passage:
"Preeti! You picked up!"
"Zubin, it's been three months. Of course I picked up."
"I'm sorry. The job's been crazy. I kept meaning to call."
"I know. Me too, with the thesis." She paused. "Honestly, I thought we were drifting."
"We are. That's why I'm calling." He took a breath. "What if we set a thing? Every second Sunday, a call. Even ten minutes."
"That sounds like a meeting."
"A meeting with chai and gossip."
She laughed. "Okay. And if one of us cancels?"
"Then that person sends a voice note with a full update. Punishment."
"Deal."
"And when I come to Pune in May—"
"You're staying at mine. No hotel."
"Deal."

qa.q: How often did Zubin suggest they call?
qa.a: He suggested every second Sunday.

qa.q: What was Preeti feeling before Zubin's call?
qa.a: She was worried they were drifting apart and perhaps a little hurt by the three months of silence.

qa.q: Why is a regular call a good idea for keeping their friendship alive?
qa.a: A fixed small commitment, even ten minutes, makes staying in touch easier than waiting for free time that never comes.

qa.q: How might Zubin feel after the call?
qa.a: He probably feels relieved and happy that Preeti still wants to stay close, and reassured by her offer to host him.

grounding: It shows two young friends making a practical plan to keep their friendship alive despite distance and busy schedules.

passage: When I left for my first job in Hyderabad, I thought my school friendships would last forever on their own. I'm Samir. Disha and I had been best friends since Class 6. For the first year we texted every day. By the second, it was once a month. Then she got engaged, and I found out from a photo online. That stung. I realised I'd stopped asking about her life. I'd send memes, not questions. So I called her, apologised, and asked about the wedding. We talked for two hours. Now we have a shared playlist and add songs every week, and I actually put her birthday in my calendar. I flew back for her wedding. It's not the same as school, but it's real.

qa.q: How did Samir find out Disha got engaged?
qa.a: Samir found out from a photo online.

qa.q: Why did finding out from a photo sting Samir?
qa.a: It made Samir realise how far they had drifted, and that Samir was no longer part of her important moments.

qa.q: What changes helped Samir and Disha stay close?
qa.a: Samir apologised, asked real questions instead of sending memes, and they started small shared habits like a weekly playlist.

qa.q: How might Disha have felt when Samir called and apologised?
qa.a: She may have been relieved and happy that Samir still cared, since they talked for two hours.

grounding: A young adult reflects on letting a close friendship drift across distance and taking steps to sustain it.

passage:
Hostel warden's note, final year:
Karthik and Hrithik were roommates for three years and very close. This year Hrithik moved off campus for an internship, and Karthik seemed low; he mentioned that Hrithik was always "too busy" to reply. I suggested he try something small and concrete rather than waiting. He decided to invite Hrithik for Saturday breakfast at the mess, like old times.
Hrithik came, a bit late and tired. They sat together for an hour, and I heard them laughing. Afterwards, Karthik told me Hrithik had been feeling guilty and overwhelmed, not uninterested.
Follow-up: they now have breakfast every other Saturday. Karthik seems more settled.

qa.q: What did Karthik invite Hrithik for?
qa.a: He invited him for Saturday breakfast at the mess.

qa.q: What had Hrithik been feeling, according to Karthik?
qa.a: He had been feeling guilty and overwhelmed, not uninterested in the friendship.

qa.q: Why was the warden's suggestion useful?
qa.a: A small, concrete invitation was easier for a busy friend to accept than waiting for replies, and it led to an honest talk.

qa.q: How might Hrithik see the regular breakfasts?
qa.a: He might feel relieved to have a simple way to stay connected despite his busy internship.

grounding: A warden's note shows young adults sustaining a friendship across new schedules with small regular plans.

passage:
Tuesday, 11:40 pm
Sabina's voice note came at lunch, seven minutes long, about her new lab in Pune and a landlady who hums film songs at 6 am. I listened in two parts between classes and grinned like an idiot. Then I realised I hadn't replied to her last one for nine days. Nine! Not because I don't care. Just placements, assignments, laundry, sleep. Scary how easily a four-year friendship turns into 'haha same' replies. So tonight I sent a real one back, and we fixed a thing: every second Saturday, a call while we both cook dinner, no cancelling unless someone is sick. She said, 'Deal, Karthik, and you have to show me your terrible sambar.' Wrote it in my planner in red. Friendships apparently need calendar slots now. Fine. She's worth a slot.

qa.q: What did Karthik and Sabina agree to do every second Saturday?
qa.a: Have a call while they both cook dinner, with no cancelling unless someone is sick.

qa.q: What worried Karthik on realising there had been no reply for nine days?
qa.a: Karthik was scared their four-year friendship could shrink into shallow 'haha same' replies because of busyness, not lack of care.

qa.q: Why does a fixed slot help a friendship like this?
qa.a: It stops the friendship depending on spare time, which busy weeks rarely have; a regular, easy ritual like cooking together keeps it going.

qa.q: How might Sabina have felt getting Karthik's real reply after nine days?
qa.a: Probably relieved and valued; her teasing about Karthik's sambar suggests she was glad to be back to their easy closeness 😊

grounding: Shows keeping a long friendship alive across cities and busy schedules by setting up a regular shared ritual.

passage: Every year at the Puja fair in their village near Bishnupur, Anirban and Jatin had eaten jilipi from the same stall. This year Jatin was in Surat, working night shifts at a textile unit, and Anirban was home from college alone. Their chats had shrunk to thumbs-up. On the second evening Anirban stood at the stall and felt oddly heavy. Then he recorded a voice note: the drums, the stall owner shouting, his own voice saying, "Your share is going cold, bhai." Twenty minutes later Jatin replied, voice cracking with laughter and tiredness: "I can smell it from here." They talked for forty minutes during Jatin's break. Before hanging up, they fixed something small: a voice note every Sunday, even thirty seconds, and a proper call on every festival.

qa.q: Where was Jatin working?
qa.a: In Surat, on night shifts at a textile unit.

qa.q: What was Anirban feeling at the jilipi stall on the second evening?
qa.a: Anirban felt heavy and lonely, missing Jatin at a place the two had always shared.

qa.q: Why is the Sunday voice note a realistic way to stay close?
qa.a: It is small enough to fit around night shifts and college, so it can last, with festival calls for longer talks.

qa.q: What was it like for Jatin to receive the voice note?
qa.a: Jatin, tired from night shifts, was moved and amused, laughing that he could smell the jilipi from Surat.

passage: For three Saturdays running, Tariq cancelled. First a double shift at the café in Leeds, then a group project, then a flu. Each time Alejandro replied "no worries 👍" from Valencia, and each time the thumbs-up felt a little colder. They had shared a flat for two years at university; now they barely shared a sentence. On a Sunday night Tariq finally wrote the message he had been avoiding: "I keep promising big calls and then bailing. Can we do small instead? Fifteen minutes while I walk to work on Tuesdays?" Alejandro's reply took an hour. "Honestly I thought you were drifting on purpose. Tuesdays. I'll be making lunch, you'll hear pans." The first Tuesday call lasted twenty-two minutes. Tariq arrived at work late and didn't mind at all.

qa.q: Where does Alejandro live now?
qa.a: In Valencia.

qa.q: What was Tariq feeling each time the thumbs-up arrived?
qa.a: Tariq felt guilty and uneasy, sensing the friendship cooling with every cancellation.

qa.q: Why was Tariq's new plan more likely to work than the big calls?
qa.a: Fifteen minutes during an existing walk fits around shifts and projects, so it is a promise small enough to keep.

qa.q: How had Alejandro been seeing Tariq's cancellations?
qa.a: Alejandro thought Tariq was drifting on purpose, so the cheerful replies probably hid hurt and disappointment.

grounding: Two former flatmates in different countries replace cancelled big calls with a small weekly habit.

passage: When the rota changed at the call centre in Gurugram, Dilnaz moved to nights and Tushar stayed on days. For two years they had shared the 1 p.m. canteen table and grumbled about the same customers. Now their only overlap was the ten minutes at shift change, when he was leaving and she was badging in, both too tired to talk. After a month Dilnaz noticed she no longer knew what was going on in his life. So she stuck a note inside his locker: "Samosa + 10 minutes, Friday 9:50 pm, bench by the gate?" On Friday he was there with two samosas and a flask of tea. They didn't solve anything. He told her about his sister's wedding plans; she told him about the man who had sung her a song on a complaint call. It became their Friday. Some weeks it was only five minutes.

qa.q: Where did Dilnaz suggest they meet?
qa.a: At the bench by the gate.

qa.q: How might Dilnaz have felt noticing she no longer knew what was going on in Tushar's life?
qa.a: Dilnaz probably felt a little lonely and sad, sensing the friendship slipping away because of the new shifts.

qa.q: Why did the locker note work where tired chats at shift change didn't?
qa.a: It set a small, specific time and place, Friday at the bench with samosas, so they met on purpose instead of hoping to catch each other.

qa.q: How might Tushar have felt finding the note?
qa.a: Tushar probably felt pleased and valued, since he turned up with samosas and a flask.

grounding: Two colleagues split by a shift change keep their friendship going with a short, fixed weekly meeting.

passage:
Dear Siddharth,
It's been seven months since you moved to Toronto, and I realised we haven't talked properly since your birthday. That's partly my fault. Work has eaten me alive.
I miss our Sunday chai at the stall near college. So I have an idea: first Sunday of every month, 9 p.m. my time, video call. Even twenty minutes. Even if one of us is exhausted.
I'll also send you voice notes when something reminds me of you, like the chaiwala asking where "that tall friend" went.
Friendships like ours don't just survive. We have to keep them alive on purpose.
Write back, or better, call.
Preeti

qa.a: Preeti felt guilty and missed Siddharth, worried they were drifting.

passage:
People ask how Uma and I stayed friends for ten years. I'm Kunal, by the way. Here's the honest answer: we nearly didn't.
After college, she went to Delhi, I stayed in Pune. For six months we just liked each other's posts. That's not friendship; that's being polite.
Then her father was in hospital, and I found out from a group chat. I felt awful that I hadn't known.
I called her that night. She cried. I listened.
After that, we made a rule: one real conversation a month, not just memes. We send each other a book every birthday. When I'm in Delhi, I stay at her place.
It takes effort. But she's the first person I call when anything happens.

qa.q: How long have Kunal and Uma been friends?
qa.a: Ten years.

qa.q: What was Kunal feeling on learning about Uma's father from a group chat?
qa.a: Kunal felt awful and guilty for not knowing.

qa.q: What choice inside the story turned things around?
qa.a: Kunal called Uma that night and listened, then they agreed on a monthly real conversation.

qa.q: How might Uma have felt when Kunal called that night?
qa.a: Uma probably felt comforted and less alone during her father's illness.

grounding: A young adult tells how deliberate habits kept a long-distance friendship alive.

I'm Usha, Jahnavi's roommate in Mumbai. I've watched how she keeps her school friends close even though they're all in different cities now.
Every Sunday morning, she makes coffee and does a group video call with four of them. Sometimes it's just ten minutes because someone's working. She keeps a small notebook of their birthdays and exams.
Last month one of them had a breakup. Jahnavi took a night bus to Nashik to see her.
I don't know how she does it with her job. She seems tired sometimes. But she always looks happy after those calls.

passage:
June: Vijay moved to Pune for his first job; Amandeep stayed in Chandigarh for his master's. They promised to call every week. By August, they hadn't spoken in five weeks.
September: Vijay forgot Amandeep's birthday. He saw it the next morning on social media and felt terrible. He called at lunch. Amandeep answered, a little cool. "Busy life, huh?"
"No excuse. I'm sorry. Can we fix the rhythm? Calls don't work for us."
They tried something smaller: a voice note every Sunday, even thirty seconds, about the best and worst thing of the week.
December: Vijay had nineteen voice notes saved. He knew about Amandeep's new flatmate, his bad professor, his sister's engagement. When Vijay visited home for New Year, they talked till two in the morning like nothing had changed.

qa.q: What did Vijay and Amandeep start sending every Sunday?
qa.a: A voice note, even thirty seconds, about the best and worst thing of the week.

qa.q: How did Vijay feel after forgetting Amandeep's birthday?
qa.a: Vijay felt terrible and guilty, and called at lunch to apologise.

qa.q: Why did voice notes work better than weekly calls?
qa.a: They were small enough to fit busy schedules, so the friendship kept going without needing a free hour at the same time.

qa.q: What was it like for Amandeep when Vijay forgot the birthday?
qa.a: Amandeep was likely hurt and felt forgotten, which showed in the cool "Busy life, huh?"

passage:
Keerthana, you think your school friends will vanish now that you're all in different cities? Let me tell you about Latha and me.
We met at college in Madurai when we were eighteen. Then I married and moved to Delhi, and she went to the Gulf with her husband. No phones then, only letters and expensive trunk calls.
For the first year I wrote every month, and she didn't reply for four months. I was so hurt I nearly stopped. Then her letter came: her baby had been ill. She had read mine every night. I decided then: I would keep writing, even if replies were slow.
Thirty-two years, Keerthana. Letters, then emails, then video calls. She came to your mother's wedding.
So write to your friends even when they're slow. That's what your Sarita Athai learned.

qa.q: Where did Latha move with her husband?
qa.a: Latha went to the Gulf with her husband.

qa.q: How did young Sarita feel when Latha didn't reply for four months?
qa.a: Young Sarita felt hurt and nearly gave up writing.

qa.q: What was the turning point in the friendship, and why did it matter?
qa.a: Latha's letter explaining her baby's illness showed that silence wasn't rejection, so Sarita chose to keep writing even when replies were slow.

qa.q: How might Latha have felt reading Sarita's letters during her baby's illness?
qa.a: Latha probably felt comforted and less alone, reading them every night even though she couldn't reply.

grounding: Shows an elder recounting how she sustained a friendship across distance over decades.

passage:
Hansa worked night shifts at a hospital lab in Bengaluru. Chaitanya was in his final year of engineering, buried in a project. They had been best friends since school, and for three months they'd only exchanged memes.
One morning, Hansa, walking out of her shift at 7 a.m., saw a message: "Do you even exist anymore?" It stung. Then she realised he was right.
She called. "My schedule is a mess. Yours too. What's one thing we can actually keep?"
They worked it out. Sunday at 8 a.m., before she slept and before his day started, they'd walk together in Cubbon Park for twenty minutes. If one of them couldn't, a two-line message was enough.
Some Sundays one of them yawned the whole way. But they kept it. By the end of the year, it was the part of the week they both protected first.

qa.q: Where did Hansa and Chaitanya walk on Sundays?
qa.a: In Cubbon Park, for twenty minutes.

qa.q: How did Hansa feel when she read "Do you even exist anymore?"
qa.a: Hansa felt stung and a little guilty, realising Chaitanya had a point.

qa.q: What made their plan work despite busy schedules?
qa.a: They chose a short, fixed time that suited both, and allowed a two-line message when they couldn't, so the plan was realistic.

qa.q: What was it like for Chaitanya during the three months of memes?
qa.a: Chaitanya likely felt lonely and missed his friend, which is why he sent the frustrated message.

grounding: Illustrates two young adults keeping a friendship alive around night shifts and heavy workloads.

passage: Chinmay found the photo while clearing his gallery on the Bengaluru metro: him and Darshan at the college canteen, both covered in Holi colour, a year and a half ago. Their last real conversation had been a thumbs-up in April. Now it was July. He typed "hey, long time" and deleted it, feeling faintly guilty. Darshan was in Kolkata now, working night shifts at a call centre; Chinmay had a new job and a flatmate who cooked at midnight. Neither of them had stopped caring. They had just stopped making time. At his stop, Chinmay sent a voice note instead: "Found this. I miss your terrible jokes. Can we fix a call, Sunday mornings, even fifteen minutes?" The reply came that night, a laughing voice note and one line: "Sunday 10. I'll set an alarm."

qa.q: When did Chinmay and Darshan agree to talk?
qa.a: On Sunday at 10, a fixed Sunday morning call.

qa.q: Why did Chinmay delete his first message?
qa.a: He felt faintly guilty about months of silence, and a bare "hey, long time" seemed too thin to fix that.

qa.q: What small step helped restart the friendship?
qa.a: A warm, specific voice note with a shared photo and a short, fixed Sunday call turned vague good intentions into a routine.

qa.q: How might Darshan feel receiving the voice note after months of silence?
qa.a: Darshan probably feels delighted and relieved to be missed, judging by the laughing reply and the promise to set an alarm 😊

grounding: Shows a young adult reviving a friendship that distance and busy schedules had let slide.
